implementation_notes: The Ruby realization is an accessor that memoizes: `@conn ||= connect(cfg)`. Ruby's abbreviated assignment assigns only when the current value is nil or false and short-circuits before evaluating the right-hand side, so the acquisition runs at most once per object (the core assignment page documents both ||= and &&=). Because it is a read-modify-write it is not atomic: the GVL can switch threads inside the acquisition, so a holder shared across threads needs Mutex#synchronize plus a second check inside the lock, and instance_variable_defined? (or a sentinel) when nil/false is a legitimate value. Enumerator::Lazy covers the different, sequence-level sense of lazy - deferring element computation, not resource acquisition - and concurrent-ruby's Delay/Promises provide the deferred-value form for threaded code.
pitfalls: ||= cannot distinguish not-yet-acquired from an acquired nil or false: if the resource value can be nil, every call re-acquires - use defined?(@x)/instance_variable_defined? and assign explicitly.
Read-modify-write is not atomic across threads: two threads entering the accessor together can each open a connection and one is leaked; guard with Mutex#synchronize and re-check inside the lock.
Memoization writes an instance variable, so a frozen receiver raises FrozenError on first use - a failure that appears only in production, when the object was frozen elsewhere.
Class-level memoization (a class-body ||= or @@x ||=) is shared by every instance and is a classic multi-threaded server race: per-instance state belongs in the instance.
